title: Prehistoric survivor growing in Syke herb garden has roots stretching back 300 million years
excerpt: Residents picking herbs from a community garden in Syke are being invited to help tackle horsetail — a persistent weed whose ancestors grew locally more than 300 million years ago.
body:
A troublesome weed growing in a community herb garden in Syke has a remarkable connection to the landscape's prehistoric past — with its ancestors dating back more than 300 million years.

Residents are being encouraged to help maintain the community herb garden while collecting fresh herbs to take home.

The garden is open for people to pick herbs for their own use, but volunteers are asking visitors who have a few spare minutes to lend a hand with some weeding at the same time.

One plant in particular is proving difficult to control: horsetail, also commonly known as mare's tail.

While modern gardeners may regard it as a persistent nuisance, horsetail belongs to an extraordinarily ancient group of plants whose history stretches back to long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.

During the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago, relatives of today's horsetails grew across the landscapes that would eventually become northern England.

Among them were Calamites — tree-like plants related to modern horsetails which could grow many metres tall and formed part of the vast Carboniferous vegetation.

Evidence of that lost landscape can still be found locally. A fossil discovered in a quarry at Tonacliffe shows the distinctive remains of Calamites, providing a physical connection between the plants growing here hundreds of millions of years ago and the much smaller horsetails residents battle in gardens today.

Carboniferous plant fossils can also be found within rocks across the surrounding moorland, reflecting a period when the area's environment looked dramatically different from the Pennine landscape residents know today.

People remain welcome to collect herbs from the community garden, but anyone visiting is being encouraged to pull a few weeds while they are there.

As the volunteers joked, nobody wants today's horsetail growing to the size of its Carboniferous grandparents.

The community garden is maintained for local people to enjoy, and even a few minutes of weeding can help keep it productive and accessible for everyone.

title: Full house for National Emergency Briefing screening in Falinge
excerpt: A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with Rochdale councillors Tricia Ayrton and Shah Wazir joining residents for the event and discussion afterwards.
body:
A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with two Rochdale Council portfolio holders joining residents for the event and subsequent discussion.

Organisers have thanked everyone who attended the screening, saying it was encouraging to see such a strong turnout for the film and the conversation which followed.

Rochdale Borough Council portfolio holders Councillor Tricia Ayrton and Councillor Shah Wazir were among those attending.

Organisers thanked both councillors for remaining after the screening to listen to residents, take part in discussions and consider how the issues raised by the film could be discussed more widely.

They said the councillors left the event with a plan to help ensure the film and its message reach a broader audience.

The National Emergency Briefing brings together scientists, campaigners and public figures to discuss climate change and the risks they believe the UK faces, with contributors associated with the project including environmental campaigner Chris Packham.

The Falinge event gave residents an opportunity not only to watch the presentation together but to discuss its arguments and what they could mean at a local level.

Following the strong turnout, another community screening has already been arranged.

The next screening will take place on Thursday, September 4 at 6pm, giving residents who were unable to attend the latest event another opportunity to see the film and join the discussion.

Organisers thanked residents, guests and councillors for supporting the event and helping create what they described as an important community conversation.
